analysis.one_liner: Requires chemical plants to protect against criminal attacks and switch to safer technologies where practicable.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 1999 with no cosponsors, never got a committee hearing or vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written chemical plant security into the Clean Air Act. Within a year, the Attorney General would have had to decide whether chemical plants were doing enough to prevent a criminal or terrorist release of dangerous chemicals. If not, the Justice Department could have written binding rules requiring plants to use less hazardous processes where practical, harden their sites against intruders, train workers, and put buffer zones between chemical facilities and nearby homes, schools, and hospitals.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near chemical plants — the populations most exposed if a toxic, flammable, or explosive chemical is released by sabotage, theft, or attack. The bill's own findings cite the FBI and the federal toxic substances agency on the seriousness of the threat, and argue that safer technologies can lower the danger while also saving plants money on security, containment, and insurance.

how_it_helps.text: Would have added a legal duty for chemical plant owners to identify and prevent releases caused by criminal acts, on top of the existing duty for accidental releases [S3].

Would have directed the Attorney General, within one year, to judge whether plants have taken adequate actions to detect, prevent, and minimize criminal releases, and to write binding security requirements if they have not [S2] [S3].

Would have defined 'safe facilities' to include using inherently safer technology — less hazardous inputs, simpler processes, smaller chemical inventories — before relying on fences, guards, and buffer zones [S3].

Would have required buffer zones between chemical facilities and residences, schools, hospitals, senior centers, shopping centers, arenas, and roads, to reduce consequences of any release that still occurred [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical plant owners and operators. They would bear the cost of hazard assessments, security upgrades, employee training, and — where required — redesigning processes to use less dangerous substances, moderating pressures and temperatures, and holding smaller chemical inventories.

drawbacks.text: Mandating redesign toward inherently safer technology could impose significant capital costs on chemical plants, and the bill leaves 'maximum extent practicable' to be defined by regulators rather than statute, creating compliance uncertainty [S3].

The bill puts the Attorney General in charge of industrial safety rules, an unusual assignment; whether the Justice Department has the technical capacity to set chemical plant design standards is a fair question the bill leaves unanswered [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is straightforward: protection for the communities surrounding roughly 15,000+ regulated chemical facilities in exchange for compliance costs borne by plant owners. The bill's own findings argue the trade is not purely one-sided — it cites industry savings on security, containment, buffer zones, and insurance from safer processes [S3]. The main design weakness is enforcement through the Attorney General rather than EPA, and open-ended regulatory discretion. On the merits, the public benefit of preventing a toxic release in a populated area would outweigh typical compliance costs; the bill never got far enough for anyone to test that claim.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — never reported out, never debated, never voted on.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on July 30, 1999, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical plant owners came out ahead: no security assessments, no inherently safer technology requirements, no buffer zones, and no compliance costs were ever imposed. Communities near chemical facilities got nothing. The bill's premise resurfaced after the 2001 terrorist attacks, when chemical plant security again became a national issue — but that later fight is a different bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical plant owners avoided new mandates

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for Clean Air Act amendments
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no report to the floor

against.name: Chemical manufacturing industry
against.role: Industry that would bear the bill's compliance costs
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory chemical security and inherently safer technology requirements during this era, favoring voluntary industry programs instead

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one cosponsored, so no party-line pattern exists in the record; the bill died before any position beyond the sponsor's was on the table.

industries.note: The bill would have required vulnerability assessments, security measures, and where practicable redesign toward less hazardous processes, plus buffer zones near population centers. The industry's savings on this bill are the public's protection; its interest in blocking the mandate ran directly against the safety of nearby communities.

industries.industry: Environmental and security consulting and equipment firms
industries.note: Hazard assessments, hardened facilities, monitoring equipment, and secondary containment requirements would create demand for security engineering and compliance services.
